chunks: Changing or resolving an I2C target address. The question: How can you change a slave's address?
Two I2C chips must not answer to the same address, or both respond at once and corrupt each other. Sometimes you can pick different addresses with pins on the chip.
Some chips let software write a new address. If a chip's address is fixed, you can keep the two apart with a multiplexer or a second bus instead.
Imagine two houses on a street with the same number. The mail carrier can't tell them apart. You have several fixes. Choose different numbers when building, which is the pins.
Repaint one number later, which is a programmable register. Or put the houses on different streets, which is a multiplexer or a second bus.
Repainting has a catch: if the paint washes off whenever the power goes off, you must repaint each time.
The same part number twice. ADC #1 has ADDR tied to ground (0x48); ADC #2 has ADDR tied to VDD (0x49).
For a part like TI's ADS1115, tying ADDR to SDA or SCL gives 0x4 amps and 0x4B, so four copies can share a bus.
(Values quoted from the commonly used device family; confirm in the datasheet.)
Address-select pin: a pin you tie to ground, supply or another level to choose one of a few addresses for the chip ("I2C address and data frames").
Default address: the address a chip answers to right after power-up. Programmable address: a register where firmware can write a new address.
Volatile: lost when power is removed, so it must be set again at every start. Enable pin: a pin that keeps a chip switched off until you release it.
Multiplexer: a chip that connects one of several side-branches to the main bus ("How many targets fit on an I2C bus").
Four identical sensors all answer at 0x29 when powered. Each has an enable pin. Hold three disabled and release the first. Write its new address, 0x30.
Release the second and write 0x31, and so on. Now all four have unique addresses, though you must repeat the routine at every power-up.
A fixed-address chip needs a multiplexer instead. With three address pins, each tied high or low, a chip has 2 to the 3 equals 8 addresses.
Behind an 8-channel multiplexer, you can reach 8 times 8 equals 64 such chips. That is the whole idea.
"Usually you don't change it in firmware; you set it in hardware. Many parts have address pins strapped to ground, supply, SDA or SCL to pick among two to eight addresses.
Some parts have a programmable address register, so with identical parts you use their enable pins to bring them up one at a time and give each a new address.
If neither is possible, isolate them with an I2C multiplexer or a second bus. SMBus ARP and I3C also assign addresses dynamically."
